Infinity means endlessness — a quantity, size, or extent that has no limit and cannot be exhausted, no matter how long you keep going.

It is not simply "a very large number." It is the absence of any boundary or stopping point whatsoever. This is a crucial distinction. A very large number, like a trillion trillion, is still finite — you can eventually reach it, count past it, and go further. Infinity is different in kind, not just in degree. It is the concept that there is no largest value to reach at all.
Infinity is a concept, not a number

This is the single most important thing to understand about infinity: it is not a number you can calculate with in the ordinary sense. It is a mathematical and philosophical concept — the idea of something that never ends.

In everyday arithmetic, numbers behave in predictable ways:

  • 5 + 1 = 6
  • 10 − 3 = 7
  • 8 × 2 = 16

But infinity doesn't behave like that. Consider these:

  • Infinity + 1 = still infinity (adding 1 to something endless doesn't make it "more endless")
  • Infinity − infinity = undefined (you can't subtract endlessness from endlessness and get a reliable answer)
  • Infinity × 2 = still infinity
  • Infinity ÷ Infinity = undefined (not 1, not anything predictable)

These results feel strange because we're used to numbers that sit still and behave. Infinity refuses to sit still. It's a moving horizon — the moment you think you've reached it, it's still infinitely far ahead.
The simplest examples of infinity

Natural numbers: Start counting: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5… Can you reach a point where you must stop because there is no next number? No. There is always n+1. The counting numbers go on forever. This is the most intuitive example of infinity in mathematics.

A number line: Imagine a straight line extending in both directions. Pick any two points on it, say 0 and 1. Between just those two points, how many numbers exist? Infinitely many: 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.5, 0.333…, 0.7182…, and so on without end. You can always find another number squeezed between any two numbers, no matter how close together they are.

Space: If the universe is infinite, then no matter how far you travel in any direction, there is always more space beyond — no wall, no edge, no "you've reached the end" sign.
Not all infinities are the same size

This is one of the most astonishing mathematical discoveries, made by the mathematician Georg Cantor in the 19th century: some infinities are larger than others.

Here is how to understand it:

Imagine matching every natural number (1, 2, 3, 4…) with every even number (2, 4, 6, 8…). Even though even numbers seem like "half" of all numbers, you can pair them up perfectly — 1 with 2, 2 with 4, 3 with 6, and so on forever. Neither list runs out first. So these two infinite sets are the same size of infinity.

This type of infinity — where things can be paired up one-to-one with the natural numbers — is called countably infinite. You can, in principle, list them out one by one forever (even if you never finish).

But now consider all the real numbers between 0 and 1 — every decimal like 0.4728361… with digits going on forever in every possible combination. Cantor proved, using a clever logical argument, that no matter how you try to list these numbers, there will always be real numbers left out. They cannot be paired up with the natural numbers. There are simply "too many" of them.

This second type of infinity is called uncountably infinite, and it is a strictly larger infinity than the first kind.

So infinity is not one single thing — it comes in different magnitudes. Mathematicians use the term cardinality to refer to the "size" of an infinite set, and there is an entire hierarchy of infinities, each one vastly larger than the one before.
The symbol for infinity

The infinity symbol is ∞, resembling a sideways figure-eight. It appears in mathematics, physics, and computing to represent a value that grows without bound or a quantity that has no finite limit. It was introduced by the mathematician John Wallis in 1655.
Infinity in mathematics — key appearances

Limits: In calculus, mathematicians often ask: "What value does a quantity approach as something grows without bound?" For example, as x gets larger and larger without stopping, 1/x gets closer and closer to 0. We say the limit as x approaches infinity is 0. Infinity here is used as a direction of travel, not a destination you actually arrive at.

Sums of infinite series: You can sometimes add up infinitely many numbers and get a finite result. For example:
½ + ¼ + ⅛ + 1/16 + … (each term is half the previous one)
This infinite sum equals exactly 1. The terms shrink fast enough that the total doesn't explode. This is called a convergent infinite series.

But sometimes an infinite sum grows without bound:
1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + … = infinity (divergent — it never settles)

Infinite sets: A set is just a collection of things. The set of all even numbers is infinite. The set of all points on a line is infinite. Set theory — the branch of mathematics dealing with collections — is where the deepest and most rigorous study of infinity lives.
Infinity in physics and the real world

In physics, infinity often signals that something has gone wrong in the math — a place where a theory breaks down and gives a nonsensical answer.

For example, in the equations of general relativity (which describes gravity), the center of a black hole produces a mathematical result of infinite density and infinite curvature of space. Physicists call this a singularity. It doesn't mean there is literally infinite density there — it means the theory stops working at that point, and a better theory (likely a future theory of quantum gravity) is needed.

In contrast, the universe itself may or may not be spatially infinite — we genuinely don't know. What we can observe is limited by how far light has had time to travel since the Big Bang. Whether space itself continues forever beyond what we can see is an open question in cosmology.
Infinity in philosophy

Philosophers have wrestled with infinity for thousands of years.

Potential vs. actual infinity: The ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle made a distinction that stayed influential for centuries. He accepted potential infinity — the idea that you can always take one more step, that a process can always continue. But he rejected actual infinity — the idea that a truly infinite collection can exist as a completed whole all at once. He believed actual infinity was incoherent.

Modern mathematics, especially since Cantor, embraces actual infinity. Mathematicians routinely work with infinite sets as complete objects, not just ongoing processes.

Zeno's paradoxes: Zeno of Elea posed famous puzzles about infinity and motion. The most well-known: to walk from point A to point B, you must first walk half the distance. Then half of what remains. Then half again — infinitely many steps. How can you ever arrive? The resolution, understood through calculus, is that an infinite number of steps can take a finite amount of time if the steps themselves shrink fast enough.
Infinity in everyday language

Outside of mathematics, people use "infinity" more loosely to mean an overwhelmingly large, uncountable amount — not literally mathematical infinity, but a rhetorical gesture at vastness:

  • "I have infinity things to do today." (A lot of tasks)
  • "She has infinite patience." (Remarkably great patience)
  • "The possibilities are infinite." (Meaning: too many to count, or "the field is wide open")

These uses are figurative. They don't claim strict mathematical infinity — they use the word as a powerful intensifier.
Common misconceptions, cleared up

"Infinity is the biggest number." No. Infinity is not a number at all. No matter how large a number you name, it is still finite — still a specific, reachable point on the number line. Infinity is what lies beyond any and all specific numbers.

"Infinity plus one is bigger than infinity." In everyday intuition this feels true, but in formal mathematics it depends on what kind of infinity you mean and in what framework you're working. For the most basic types of infinite sets (countably infinite ones), ∞ + 1 is the same size of infinity. Adding a finite amount to an already-infinite collection doesn't change its cardinality.

"Infinity is just a very large number." This misses the fundamental difference in kind. A very large number can be doubled, halved, and compared with other numbers on equal footing. Infinity is a concept that represents the absence of any upper boundary, which is a fundamentally different thing.

"There is only one infinity." As Cantor showed, there is a whole tower of infinities. The infinity of the natural numbers is smaller than the infinity of the real numbers, which is smaller than even larger infinities that mathematicians construct — and this hierarchy never ends.
The big picture

Infinity is one of the most profound and genuinely strange ideas in all of human thought. It sits at the heart of mathematics (calculus, set theory, number theory), physics (cosmology, singularities), and philosophy (the nature of space, time, and existence). It is the concept that some things — sequences, sets, extents — have no end, no bound, no final element. It challenges our intuitions built from a world of finite, tangible things. And yet, mathematicians have developed rigorous tools to reason about it with complete precision.

The key things to hold onto:

  • Infinity means without end or limit
  • It is a concept, not an ordinary number
  • Different infinities can be different sizes
  • It appears naturally in counting, geometry, calculus, physics, and philosophy
  • In everyday speech it's used loosely to mean "an enormous, uncountable amount"
